answers_by_date.answer: any conviction (even minor administrative offenses) can lead to loss of residence status
answers_by_date.basis: DL 1.094 art. 64 allowed refusal of applications for persons 'condenados en Chile por crimen o simple delito' (No. 1) and for those who breach the decree's obligations (No. 5). Art. 66 allowed revocation on any art. 64 ground, and arts. 17 and 84 provided for expulsion. These articles were unchanged 2000-2020. Practice evidence is not needed because this is the lowest option.

answers_by_date.answer: any conviction (even minor administrative offenses) can lead to loss of residence status
answers_by_date.basis: Same DL 1.094 arts. 63-67, 17 and 84, with no relevant amendment between 2000 and 2005.

answers_by_date.answer: any conviction (even minor administrative offenses) can lead to loss of residence status
answers_by_date.basis: Same regime. Ley 20.430 (April 2010) touched only the refugee provisions, and came after this date.

answers_by_date.answer: any conviction (even minor administrative offenses) can lead to loss of residence status
answers_by_date.basis: Same arts. 64 and 66. Ley 20.507 (in force 2011-04-08) added migrant smuggling and trafficking to art. 15 No. 2, a ground for refusal and revocation under arts. 63 and 65. This widened the grounds.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been no right protections neither in 2000 nor in 2020

events.what_changed: Added migrant smuggling and trafficking in persons to the grounds that bar entry and lead to revocation and expulsion. This widened the conviction-related grounds and did not protect status.

answers.repealed_search: I checked the consolidated DL 1.094 with its marginal amendment notes for any provision that once protected residence status after a conviction. Arts. 63-66 carry no amendment notes, so they kept their 1975 wording; art. 67 was amended only in 1983 (Ley 18.252). I found no protection that was repealed between 2000 and 2020.
answers.sourcing_note: I read the last consolidated text of DL 1.094 on LeyChile, whose margin notes name each amending law. The per-date version pages and Ley 19.806 (2002) were not opened, but arts. 63-66 show no amendment notes.
answers.notes: Before 2022 the loss of status rested on DL 1.094 art. 64 No. 1 (conviction for a crimen or simple delito) and No. 5 (breach of the decree's obligations), with revocation under art. 66.

answers_by_date.basis: DL 1.094 art. 39 (Ley 19.476, 1996) barred expelling refugees and asylum seekers only to a country where life or freedom was at risk on the five Convention grounds. It did not mention torture. Chile has ratified the Convention against Torture, but no statute incorporated its art. 3.
Same. Ley 20.430 was published on 2010-04-15, after this date.

Ley 20.430 art. 4 inciso 2 (from 2010-04-15) bans return of asylum seekers and refugees where there are grounds to believe they would face torture. The MRD's starting answer treats this as not covering migrants generally, so this date keeps the starting answer.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been no right protections neither in 2000 nor in 2020

provisions.instrument: Ley 20.430, Establece disposiciones sobre protección de refugiados

events.what_changed: Replaced DL 1.094 art. 39 with a broader non-refoulement rule that covers torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment for asylum seekers and refugees.
events.passage: cualquier forma de devolución hacia las fronteras de un país donde estuviere en peligro la seguridad de la persona o existieren razones fundadas para creer que podría ser sometida a tortura, a tratos o penas crueles, inhumanos o degradantes.

answers.repealed_search: I searched DL 1.094 (arts. 34-40 bis) for a torture-based ban that might have been repealed before 2020. Art. 39 covered only the five Convention grounds. No repealed torture protection was found; the 2010 law broadened the protection.
answers.sourcing_note: I read the consolidated texts of DL 1.094 and Ley 20.430. Art. 4 carries no amendment notes. Per-date versions were not opened.
answers.starting_answer_concern: Ley 20.430 art. 4 inciso 2 expressly bans return to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, for asylum seekers as well as recognised refugees. The MRD citation's claim that only recognised refugees are covered is wrong, so from 2010-04-15 a 'Yes' limited to asylum seekers and refugees looks arguable.
answers.notes: Before 2010 DL 1.094 had no torture ground, so No is solid for 2000 and 2005 under either reading.

answers_by_date.basis: DL 1.094 art. 39 (Ley 19.476): a refugee or political asylee may not be expelled to a country where life or freedom is at risk on the five grounds, and nor may asylum seekers while their claim is pending. The US State Department report on 1999 found 'no reports of the forced return of persons to a country where they feared persecution'. Caseloads were very small.
Same art. 39. The US State Department report on 2004 says the government 'provided protection against refoulement', with 568 recognised refugees.
Same art. 39; Ley 20.430 replaced it on 2010-04-15. The US State Department report on 2009 says the government protected refugees against return on persecution grounds.

Ley 20.430 arts. 3 and 4 ban return of asylum seekers and refugees and expressly ban rejection at the border. The US State Department report on 2014 reports no refoulement. Reports of informal pre-admissibility screening were not read.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 but they are not the same

events.what_changed: Replaced DL 1.094 art. 39 (no expulsion of refugees or asylum seekers to persecution) with art. 4, which bans any measure of return, including rejection at the border.
events.passage: No procederá la expulsión o cualquier medida que tenga por efecto la devolución, incluyendo la prohibición de ingreso en frontera, de un solicitante de la condición de refugiado o refugiado al país donde su vida o libertad personal peligren.

events.what_changed: This 1996 wording was in force throughout 2000-2010.
events.passage: Un refugiado o asilado político no podrá ser expulsado hacia el país donde su vida o libertad peligre por causa de su raza, religión, nacionalidad, pertenencia a determinados grupos sociales u opiniones políticas.

answers.sourcing_note: Law: consolidated texts read, with dates taken from LeyChile's amendment notes. Practice: only the US State Department reports were read. NGO and UDP reports (PDFs) could not be opened, so evidence for 2015 is thin.
answers.notes: The protection was Yes throughout, but its basis changed in 2010 from DL 1.094 art. 39 to Ley 20.430 art. 4, which adds the border-rejection ban, hence 'not the same'. The fall to 'Sometimes' by 2020 reflects border practice in 2017-2019 that I did not examine here. The 2015 rating could be overstated.

answers_by_date.basis: DL 1.094 art. 39 covered only the five persecution grounds. Nothing barred return on the basis of generalised violence or massive human-rights violations.

Ley 20.430 art. 2(2) (Cartagena-type definition) and art. 4 inciso 3 (massive human-rights violations) cover asylum seekers and refugees only. Following the starting answer, this is No for migrants generally.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been no right protections neither in 2000 nor in 2020

events.what_changed: Introduced the Cartagena-type refugee definition, which covers threats to life from generalised violence and massive human-rights violations. Non-refoulement now applies to such cases, but only for asylum seekers and refugees.
events.passage: cuya vida, seguridad o libertad han sido amenazadas por la violencia generalizada, la agresión extranjera, los conflictos internos, la violación masiva de los derechos humanos

answers.repealed_search: I searched DL 1.094 arts. 34-40 bis and Ley 20.507 (art. 33 bis: no repatriation of trafficking victims at grave risk to their physical or psychological integrity, from 2011-04-08) for any broader protection that was later repealed. None was found. Art. 33 bis covers only trafficking victims and was not repealed before 2020.
answers.sourcing_note: Consolidated texts of DL 1.094 and Ley 20.430 were read. Version pages for each date were not opened.
answers.starting_answer_concern: From 2010, Ley 20.430 arts. 2(2) and 4 protect asylum seekers and refugees against return to massive human-rights violations. A conditional 'Yes' is arguable if the indicator is read as applying to those seeking protection.
answers.notes: From 2011, DL 1.094 art. 33 bis (Ley 20.507) also barred repatriating trafficking victims at grave risk. It is narrow and does not change the answer.
